title: Parts of Speech
sub: 先備概念：先認識英文的八種「字的工作」，之後每一課都會用到。The eight word jobs — the map for everything that follows.

form.p: Every word has a job: naming, doing, describing or joining.

uses.d: A noun names a person, place, thing or idea. A pronoun stands in for a noun so we don't repeat it.

ex.n: an idea is a noun too

ex.s: Ben is tired, so he went to bed.

uses.t: Doing & describing words: verbs, adjectives, adverbs
uses.d: A verb shows an action or a state. An adjective describes a noun. An adverb describes a verb (and often ends in -ly).

uses.t: Little joining & pointing words: prepositions, conjunctions, interjections
uses.d: A preposition shows place or time (in, on, under, before). A conjunction joins ideas (and, but, because). An interjection shows sudden feeling (Wow! Oh!).

ex.s: I was tired, but I finished the work.

mistakes.why: To describe a verb (sings) you need an adverb, not an adjective.

mistakes.no: He is a quick runner and runs quick.
mistakes.yes: He is a quick runner and runs quickly.
mistakes.why: quick describes the noun runner; quickly describes the verb runs.
a/an are articles — a small kind of adjective; use an before a vowel sound.

tip: Ask what job the word does: names it (noun), replaces it (pronoun), does it (verb), describes a noun (adjective) or a verb (adverb), or joins/points (preposition, conjunction, interjection). 這一課學會了，後面每一課都更容易。

q.q: In 'Birds sing every morning', which word is the verb?
q.why: sing is the action word → verb.

q.q: In 'The old house is empty', which word is an adjective?
q.why: old describes the noun house → adjective.
It describes the verb sang → adverb.

q.q: Which word is a preposition? 'The ball rolled under the car.'
How many pronouns are in 'They gave it to us'?
'I run daily' and 'I went for a run.' The word 'run' is…
q.why: Same word, different jobs: run (verb) and a run (noun).

q.q: A word that names a person, place, thing or idea is a ___ .
q.why: Nouns name people, places, things and ideas.
They join words or ideas → conjunctions.

q.sent: He drives careful in the rain .
q.why: An adverb describes the verb drives → carefully.

q.sent: That was a real good movie .
q.why: To describe the adjective good, use the adverb really.

q.sent: The tired children slept quietly
q.why: tired (adjective) describes children; quietly (adverb) describes slept.

title: Nouns
sub: Naming words — people, places, things and ideas — plus common vs proper nouns and capital letters.

form.p: A noun names a person, place, thing or idea.

uses.d: A common noun is a general name (city, dog). A proper noun is a specific name and starts with a capital letter (Taipei, Rex).

ex.n: languages and days are proper nouns

uses.d: Concrete nouns are things you can see or touch (apple, rain). Abstract nouns are ideas or feelings (hope, danger).

uses.t: Nouns can be one or many
uses.d: Most nouns add -s to mean more than one. (Full plural rules come in Unit 2.)

mistakes.why: I and proper nouns (Taipei) need capital letters.
Languages are proper nouns — capitalize them.
Abstract nouns like advice are usually uncountable — no -s.

tip: If you can put 'a', 'the' or a number in front of it, it's probably a noun. Names of people, places, days and languages get a capital letter.

q.q: Which word is a noun? 'The children played happily.'
Which one is a proper noun?
q.why: Japan is a specific name → proper noun (capital J).

q.q: Which word is an abstract noun?
q.why: freedom is an idea you can't touch → abstract noun.

q.q: How many nouns are in 'The dog chased the ball in the park'?
The name of a country or a person is a ___ noun.
Add the capital: my friend speaks ___ . (chinese)

q.sent: We visited paris last summer .
q.why: Paris is a proper noun → capital P.

q.sent: Love is a powerful feeling
q.why: Love and feeling are nouns; powerful is an adjective.

title: Verbs
sub: Doing words and being words — the engine of every sentence.

form.p: A verb shows an action or a state. Every sentence needs a verb.

uses.d: Action verbs show a physical or a mental action.

uses.t: State / linking verbs — how things are
uses.d: Some verbs show a state, not an action: be, have, like, feel, seem. A linking verb joins the subject to a description.
Without a verb, a group of words is not a full sentence.

mistakes.no: She to the store every day.
mistakes.yes: She goes to the store every day.
mistakes.why: The sentence had no verb — add goes.
Use the verb be (am) to link I to happy.
With he / she / it, use has, not have.

tip: Ask: what is the subject doing, or how is it being? That word is the verb. No verb → not a full sentence.

q.q: Which word is the verb? 'The baby sleeps all night.'
Which group of words has NO verb?
q.why: 'A big red kite' has no verb → not a sentence.

q.q: In 'She is a teacher', the verb is…
Which is a state verb (not an action)?
q.why: know is a state of mind, not a physical action.

q.q: Add the verb: I ___ football on Sundays. (play)

q.hint: he / she / it form of have

q.sent: The children plays in the park .
q.why: children is plural → play, not plays.

q.sent: The hungry cat wants food
q.why: wants is the verb; hungry is an adjective; cat and food are nouns.

title: Adjectives & Adverbs
sub: Describing words: adjectives describe nouns, adverbs describe verbs — and how to keep them apart.

form.p: An adjective describes a noun. An adverb describes a verb, and often ends in -ly.

uses.d: An adjective tells us more about a noun — before the noun, or after be.
An adverb tells us HOW an action happens. Many are made by adding -ly to an adjective.
Most adjectives + -ly = adverb. But fast and hard don't change, and good becomes well.

mistakes.why: To describe the verb sings, use the adverb beautifully.
The adverb of good is well.
Describe the verb drive with the adverb carefully.

tip: Does the word describe a THING (noun) or an ACTION (verb)? Thing → adjective. Action → adverb (often -ly). And remember: good = adjective, well = adverb.

q.why: quiet describes the noun room → adjective.
Describing the verb dances needs the adverb gracefully.

q.sent: The children are playing quiet .
q.why: Describe the verb playing with the adverb quietly.

q.sent: The old dog barked loudly
q.why: old (adjective) describes dog; loudly (adverb) describes barked.

title: The Verb Be
sub: Am, is and are — the most common verb in English, for describing people, places and states.

form.p: subject + am / is / are + description

uses.d: Use be to say who or what someone is, or what something is like.
Be also tells us location — no other verb is needed.
Make negatives with not. Make questions by moving be before the subject.

mistakes.why: Singular jobs need a or an.
They, we and you always take are.
Be changes form: am, is, are.

tip: Match the verb to the subject: I → am · he / she / it → is · we / you / they → are.

q.why: My sister = she, so we use is.
The children = they, so we use are.

q.sent: The keys are on the table
He are my best friend .

q.why: They takes are; questions start with the verb.

q.sent: My parents is very kind .

title: Subject & Object Pronouns
sub: I, you, he, she — and me, him, her: who does the action, and who receives it.

form.p: subject pronoun + verb + object pronoun

uses.d: I, you, he, she, it, we, they do the action.

uses.t: Object pronouns — after the verb or a preposition
uses.d: Me, you, him, her, it, us, them receive the action.
Once we know who or what, a pronoun keeps the sentence light.

ex.s: Ben is my cousin. He is twelve.
I bought a cake and ate it.
Anna and I are busy — don't wait for us.

mistakes.why: Subjects use I — and name yourself last.

mistakes.no: I saw she at the mall.
mistakes.yes: I saw her at the mall.
mistakes.why: After the verb, use the object form her.

mistakes.no: Between you and I, the test was hard.
mistakes.yes: Between you and me, the test was hard.
mistakes.why: After a preposition, use me.

tip: Before the verb → subject form (I, he, she). After the verb or a preposition → object form (me, him, her).

q.why: Before the verb we need a subject pronoun.
After the verb, use the object form me.

q.q: My parents are away, so ___ am home alone.
q.why: The subject of am is always I.

q.sent: We visited them last weekend
Him is the new student in our class .

q.q: Anna and ___ are in the same class.

q.sent: I made a sandwich and ate him .
q.why: A sandwich is a thing → it.

title: Present Simple
sub: Habits, routines, facts and things that are generally true.

tl.cap: Repeated actions across time — every day, every week, always.

form.p: subject + verb(+s)  ·  he / she / it adds -s

uses.d: Things you do regularly — often with every day, usually, on Mondays.
Use it for things that are always or generally true.

uses.t: Negatives and questions with do / does
uses.d: Use do or does as a helper — and the main verb goes back to its base form.

mistakes.why: He / she / it needs verb + s.
After doesn't, use the base verb.
She takes does in questions.

tip: The -s moves, it never doubles: she works → she doesn't work → does she work?

q.sent: She usually walks to school
q.why: Frequency adverbs go before the main verb.

q.sent: My brother watch TV every night .
Does she plays tennis on Saturdays ?
q.why: After does, the verb returns to its base form.
She + doesn't + base verb is the correct pattern.

title: Present Continuous
sub: Be + V-ing — actions happening right now, or temporarily around now.

tl.cap: An action in progress at this moment — it has started and hasn't finished.

form.p: subject + am / is / are + V-ing

uses.d: The action is in progress as you speak.
Not necessarily this second — but not forever either.

ex.s: She is staying with her aunt this month.
We are learning the guitar this semester.
He is working in Taichung these days.

uses.d: Move be before the subject for questions; add not for negatives.

mistakes.why: After be, the verb needs -ing.
Don't drop be — am / is / are is required.
State verbs like know, like, want don't take -ing.

tip: Two parts, always: be (am / is / are) + V-ing. If one part is missing, the sentence is broken.

q.q: Look! The dog ___ in the river.
Please be quiet. I ___ (try) to study.

q.sent: They is playing badminton in the gym .
My mom is making dumplings now

q.why: Want is a state verb — no -ing.

q.sent: He is watch a movie with his sister .

title: Adverbs of Frequency
sub: Always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, never — saying how often.

form.p: subject + adverb + verb   ·   subject + be + adverb

uses.d: These adverbs sit on a scale from 100% down to 0%.
With normal verbs, the adverb goes just before the verb.
With am / is / are, the adverb comes after the verb instead.

ex.s: I am never bored in this class.

mistakes.why: With be, the adverb comes after the verb.

mistakes.no: I go never to the gym.
mistakes.yes: I never go to the gym.
mistakes.why: With other verbs, the adverb goes before.
Never is already negative — no double negatives.

tip: Remember: BEfore ordinary verbs, but AFTER be. Two positions, one rule each.

q.why: Adverbs of frequency follow the verb be.

q.sent: I usually have toast for breakfast
q.why: Adverb before the main verb have.

q.sent: They are never at home on Sundays
He drinks always tea in the morning .
q.why: The adverb goes before the verb: always drinks.

q.q: We ___ eat out — maybe once a month.
q.why: Once a month is rare, so rarely fits.

q.sent: I am late usually on Mondays .

title: Be Verb: Past
sub: Was and were — the past of am, is and are, for saying how things were.

form.p: subject + was / were + description

uses.t: was for I / he / she / it
uses.d: Use was with singular subjects.
Use were with plural subjects and with you.
Add not (wasn't / weren't). For questions, put was/were first.

mistakes.why: I always takes was.
They (plural) takes were.
You always takes were, even in questions.

tip: Singular (I, he, she, it) → was. Plural and you → were. It's simply the past of am / is / are.

q.sent: We were at the beach on Sunday
The weather were nice last week .
My parents was at work .

title: Have & Have Got
sub: Two ways to say what you own or what belongs to you.

form.p: subject + have / has (got) + object

uses.d: Use have with I / you / we / they, and has with he / she / it.
'have got' means the same as 'have', and is common in speaking. Use has got for he / she / it.
With have, use do / does. With have got, put have / has first.

ex.s: I don't have a car. / I haven't got a car.
Do you have a pen? / Have you got a pen?

mistakes.why: he / she / it → has.

mistakes.no: I have got not a car.
mistakes.why: The negative of 'have got' is 'haven't got'.

mistakes.no: Do you have got a pen?
mistakes.yes: Have you got a pen? / Do you have a pen?
mistakes.why: Don't mix the two question forms.

tip: he / she / it → HAS. Everyone else → HAVE. 'have got' = 'have', just more casual in speech.

q.q: I ___ have any money today. (negative helper)

q.sent: They have got a new house
Does she has a bike ?
q.why: After does, use the base form: Does she have…?

opts: Do you have got a pen?

q.sent: The house have three rooms .

title: Their / There / They're
sub: Three words that sound the same — but mean very different things.

form.p: their = of them · there = a place · they're = they are

uses.d: their is a possessive — it comes before a noun.
there points to a place, or starts 'there is / there are'.

ex.s: There is a cat on the roof.

uses.d: they're is short for 'they are'. If you can say 'they are', use they're.

mistakes.why: = they are going → they're.
belonging to them → their.
'there is' → there.

tip: their = of them (their bag). there = a place, or 'there is/are'. they're = they are. Trick: if 'they are' fits, write they're.

q.q: The children love ___ teacher. (belonging to them)

q.sent: Their going home now .
Put your bags over their .

title: Capitalization
sub: When to use a CAPITAL letter — sentences, names, days and 'I'.

form.p: Capital: sentence start · names · days/months · languages · I

uses.t: Start of a sentence, and the word 'I'
uses.d: Begin every sentence with a capital letter. Always write 'I' as a capital.

uses.t: Names of people, places & brands (proper nouns)
uses.d: Capitalize specific names: people, cities, countries, companies.
Capitalize days, months and languages/nationalities — but NOT the seasons.

mistakes.why: Capitalize the sentence start (My) and the country (France).
'I' and languages (English) are capitalized.

mistakes.no: See you on monday in Winter.
mistakes.yes: See you on Monday in winter.
mistakes.why: Days are capital (Monday), but seasons are lowercase (winter).

tip: CAPITAL for: the first word of a sentence, the word 'I', names of people/places, days, months and languages. Lowercase for seasons.

q.why: Sentence start, 'I', and the city Taipei are capital.
Days of the week are capitalized: Monday.
'I' + language English are capital; 'study' is not.

q.q: Add the capital: my birthday is in ___ . (july)

q.sent: we are going to spain in august .
q.why: Start the sentence with a capital: We. (Also Spain, August.)

q.q: Which does NOT need a capital?

q.sent: her name is maria .
q.why: Capitalize the sentence start: Her. (Also Maria.)

title: Word Order
sub: The basic order of an English sentence — subject, verb, object, and where extras go.

form.p: Subject + Verb + Object (+ place + time)

uses.d: English usually puts the subject first, then the verb, then the object.
In English, the describing word comes BEFORE the noun.

uses.t: Place before time; frequency before the verb
uses.d: Put place before time. Frequency adverbs (always, often) go before the main verb, but after be.

mistakes.no: I like very much this song.
mistakes.yes: I like this song very much.
mistakes.why: 'very much' goes after the object, at the end.
Adjectives come before the noun: a red car.

mistakes.no: I go every day to school.
mistakes.yes: I go to school every day.
mistakes.why: Place (to school) before time (every day).

tip: Subject → Verb → Object. Adjectives go BEFORE the noun. Place before time. Frequency words go before the main verb, but after be.

q.why: Adjective before the noun: a blue car.

q.sent: She reads a book every night
We went to the park yesterday
I like very much coffee .
q.why: 'very much' goes to the end: I like coffee very much.

q.q: Where does 'always' go in 'She ___ helps ___ me'?
q.why: Frequency adverbs go before the main verb: always helps.

q.sent: He has a bag black .
q.why: Adjective before the noun: a black bag.

q.q: Correct order: I / study / at the library / in the evening?
opts: I study in the evening at the library.
I study at the library in the evening.
At the library I in the evening study.
I at the library study in the evening.

zh: 句型一 S + V（主 + 不及物動詞）
title: Sentence Pattern 1: S + V
sub: Subject + intransitive verb — actions that need nothing after them.

form.p: Subject + Verb (intransitive)

uses.t: The verb is complete on its own
uses.d: Intransitive verbs don't need an object. The sentence is complete with just S + V.
You can add adverbials of place or time — but they're extras, not objects.
These verbs cannot take a direct object: go, come, arrive, sleep, fall, rise, run, smile, cry, happen.

mistakes.why: Fly is intransitive — you need a preposition (in, over, through) before the place.
'Arrive' is always followed by 'at' (for specific places) or 'in' (for cities/countries), never 'to'.
'Fall' is intransitive — it needs 'to' or 'onto' before the location.

tip: Quick test: remove everything after the verb. If the sentence still makes sense ('She smiled.' ✓ / 'She ate.' ✓), you probably have an intransitive verb — Pattern 1!

q.why: 'The baby cried' is S + V (intransitive). 'reads' takes an object, 'became' is a linking verb, and 'gave' is ditransitive.

opts: Birds fly to the sky up.
q.why: Intransitive 'fly' needs the preposition 'in' before the place.
'Sleep' needs no object. The others all take direct objects.

q.q: She arrived ___ the airport at noon.
q.why: 'Arrive at' is used for specific places (airports, stations, schools).
'Rose' is intransitive — the price just rises on its own. The others incorrectly treat intransitive verbs as transitive.

zh: 句型二 S + V + C（主 + 連綴動詞 + 補語）
title: Sentence Pattern 2: S + V + C
sub: Subject + linking verb + complement — describing what the subject is or becomes.

form.p: Subject + Linking Verb + Complement (adj / noun)

uses.d: The most common linking verb is 'be'. The complement can be a noun or an adjective.
These verbs link the subject to an adjective or noun that describes how the subject changes or appears.

uses.t: Sense verbs: look / sound / feel / taste / smell
uses.d: Sense linking verbs connect the subject to an adjective describing the sensation.

mistakes.why: After linking verbs, always use an adjective (happy), NOT an adverb (happily).
'Smell' here is a linking verb — it needs an adjective (good), not the adverb 'well'.
'Look' as a linking verb takes an adjective complement — never an adverb.

tip: Swap the linking verb with 'is / are / was / were'. If the sentence still makes sense, it's a linking verb (Pattern 2)! e.g. 'The cake looks delicious' → 'The cake IS delicious' ✓

q.q: Which sentence is Pattern 2 (S + V + C)?
q.why: 'The music sounds wonderful' = S + linking verb + adjective complement. The others are S+V+O or S+V+IO+DO.
After a linking verb like 'became', use an adjective (tired), not an adverb (tiredly).
'Seem' connects the subject to a complement (e.g. 'He seems happy'). The others are action verbs.

q.q: The milk smells ___. Don't drink it.
q.why: 'Smells' is a linking verb here, so it takes an adjective: 'bad', not the adverb 'badly'.
'They became successful' — linking verb + adjective complement. 'Calmly' / 'badly' are adverbs, and 'an engineer' needs 'is/was', not 'looks'.

zh: 句型三 S + V + O（主 + 及物動詞 + 受詞）
title: Sentence Pattern 3: S + V + O
sub: Subject + transitive verb + direct object — the most common English sentence pattern.

form.p: Subject + Transitive Verb + Object

uses.d: A transitive verb must have a direct object — it answers 'what?' or 'whom?' after the verb.
Use do/does/did to make negatives and questions with transitive verbs.
Some verbs take a gerund (V-ing) as the object; others take an infinitive (to V). This is Pattern 3 still!

mistakes.why: 'Enjoy' always takes a gerund (V-ing) as its object, not an infinitive.
'Discuss' is transitive — the object comes directly after it, no preposition needed.
Verbs like enter, reach, approach, and discuss take a direct object with NO preposition.

tip: Test: ask 'what?' or 'whom?' after the verb. If you can point to a word that answers that — that's the object, and it's Pattern 3! 'She reads __ books__' → What does she read? Books!

q.q: Which sentence is Pattern 3 (S + V + O)?
q.why: 'He bought a new phone' = S + transitive V + direct object. The others are Pattern 1, 2, and 4.
'Discuss' is a transitive verb — no preposition before the object.
'Enjoy' always takes a gerund (V-ing) as its object.

q.q: Which underlined word is the direct object?
q.why: 'A dress' is the direct object — it answers 'what did she buy?'. Options A = subject, B = verb, D = just the noun without the article.
'Enter' is transitive — the object (the room) follows directly with no preposition.

zh: 句型四 S + V + IO + DO（主 + 授與動詞 + 間接受詞 + 直接受詞）
title: Sentence Pattern 4: S + V + IO + DO
sub: Ditransitive verbs — give, send, tell, show — passing a thing (DO) to a person (IO).

form.p: Subject + Verb + Indirect Object (person) + Direct Object (thing)

uses.d: These verbs can give something to someone. The indirect object (IO = person) comes first, then the direct object (DO = thing).
You can move the IO after the DO using 'to' (give/send/show/tell/teach) or 'for' (buy/make/cook/get).

ex.s: She gave me a gift. → She gave a gift to me.
He bought her flowers. → He bought flowers for her.
She made us dinner. → She made dinner for us.

uses.d: A quick check: the indirect object is always a person (or group of people), and the direct object is usually a thing.

mistakes.no: She gave to me a gift.
mistakes.yes: She gave me a gift. / She gave a gift to me.
mistakes.why: When the IO comes before DO, there is NO preposition. 'to' only appears when the IO moves to the end.

mistakes.yes: He explained the problem to me.
mistakes.why: 'Explain' cannot have an IO before DO — it must use 'explain + DO + to + person'.

mistakes.yes: She introduced her friend to me.
mistakes.why: 'Introduce' also requires 'to' — you cannot put the person before the thing.

tip: IO is always a PERSON; DO is always a THING. Say it like a rhythm: 'Give [person] [thing]' — She gave him a book. 🎁

q.q: Which sentence is Pattern 4 (S + V + IO + DO)?
opts: She told her friend the news.
q.why: 'She told her friend the news' = S + V + IO(person) + DO(thing).
When the IO comes before the DO, there is NO 'to'. The correct form is 'She gave him a present.'
When DO comes first, 'send' uses 'to': sent flowers TO his mom.

q.q: Which verb CANNOT use S + V + IO + DO pattern?
q.why: 'Explain' must always use 'to': explain the problem TO someone. You cannot say 'explain me the problem'.

q.q: The teacher ___ the students a difficult question.
q.why: 'Ask' can follow Pattern 4: asked [IO=the students] [DO=a difficult question].

zh: 句型五 S + V + O + OC（主 + 不完全及物動詞 + 受詞 + 受詞補語）
title: Sentence Pattern 5: S + V + O + OC
sub: Causative and perception verbs — the object complement describes or renames the object.

form.p: Subject + Verb + Object + Object Complement (adj / noun)

uses.d: These verbs cause the object to be in a state. The adjective (OC) describes the object.

uses.t: call / name / elect / appoint + O + noun
uses.d: These verbs give the object a new name or title. The noun (OC) renames the object.

uses.t: Perception verbs: see / hear / watch + O + V-ing / bare infinitive
uses.d: Perception verbs use a special form for the OC: bare infinitive (one action) or V-ing (ongoing).

mistakes.why: The OC after 'make' is an adjective (happy), not an adverb (happily). It describes the object, not the verb.
'Difficulty' is a noun; 'difficult' is the adjective needed here to describe 'the test'.

mistakes.no: They named the cat to Mochi.
mistakes.why: After 'name / call / elect', the OC comes directly after the object — no preposition.

tip: Check: does the OC describe or rename the OBJECT? In 'She kept the room clean' — 'clean' describes 'the room' (the object). If yes, it's Pattern 5! 🔑

q.q: Which sentence is Pattern 5 (S + V + O + OC)?
q.why: 'He made her happy' = S + V + O + OC. 'Happy' is the object complement describing 'her'.
After 'keep + O', use an adjective (healthy) as the object complement.
Object pronouns (him, her, them) are used as objects. 'Him' is correct here.
Perception verb (saw) + O + V-ing (crossing) for an action in progress. Bare infinitive 'cross' is also correct for a completed action.
'Find + O + OC' uses an adjective. 'Boring' (adjective) describes 'the book'. Note: 'bored' would mean the book felt bored!

title: Singular & Plural Nouns
sub: Adding -s, -es and -ies — plus the irregulars everyone must memorize.

form.p: noun + s / es / ies   ·   irregular: man → men

uses.d: Most nouns just add -s. The spelling changes depend on the ending.
A small set of very common nouns change completely.
Plural subjects take plural verbs — no -s on the verb.

mistakes.why: Child has an irregular plural.
Most -o nouns add -es: tomatoes, potatoes.
People is already plural.

tip: If a noun ends in a hissing sound (s, sh, ch, x), you can't just add -s — say buses aloud and you'll hear why it needs -es.

q.q: What is the plural of city?
q.why: Consonant + y → change y to ies.

q.q: What is the plural of child?

q.sent: There are three womans in the office .

q.why: Sheep stays the same: one sheep, two sheep.

q.sent: The children are playing in the park
q.why: Children is plural, so it takes are.

q.sent: My foots hurt after the long walk .

title: This, That, These & Those
sub: Pointing words — near or far, one or many.

form.p: this / that + singular   ·   these / those + plural

uses.d: Things close to you — one takes this, many take these.

uses.t: Far from you: that and those
uses.d: Things farther away — one takes that, many take those.

ex.s: That building across the street is a library.
Those birds on the wire are sparrows.

uses.d: We also point at moments and things we just mentioned.

mistakes.why: Plural shoes → these.

mistakes.no: I want that apples over there.
mistakes.yes: I want those apples over there.
mistakes.why: Plural + far → those.
One desk → this + is.

tip: Near = this / these · Far = that / those. One = this / that · Many = these / those.

q.sent: Those bag over there is heavy .
These dumplings are delicious

q.why: On the phone, introduce yourself with this.

q.q: I didn't like ___ movie we saw last week.
q.why: Finished and far away in time → that.

q.sent: This apples taste sweet .

title: Articles: A, An, The
sub: Choosing between a, an, the — or nothing at all.

form.p: a / an + new or general (singular)   ·   the + specific or known
ex: I saw a dog. The dog was friendly.

uses.t: A and an: something new or general
uses.d: Use a before consonant sounds and an before vowel sounds — it's about the sound, not the letter.

ex.n: any bicycle, not a specific one
hour starts with a vowel sound

uses.d: Use the when the listener knows exactly which one you mean — or when there is only one.

ex.s: I saw a movie. The movie was long.

uses.t: No article: plurals and ideas in general
uses.d: Drop the article for plural or uncountable nouns used generally, and for most names.

mistakes.why: Singular jobs need a or an.
Hour begins with a vowel sound.
Abstract ideas in general take no article.

tip: Listen, don't look: a university (yoo-), an hour (ow-). The sound after the article decides a or an.

q.why: Honest starts with a vowel sound (the h is silent).

q.q: I bought a shirt and a hat. ___ shirt was expensive.
It's ___ university with a long history.
q.hint: Listen to the first sound of university
q.why: University starts with a 'yoo' consonant sound → a.
There is only one moon → the.

q.sent: My uncle is doctor in Kaohsiung .

q.why: Music in general is uncountable — no article.

q.sent: The dog in the garden is mine
We waited for a hour at the station .
q.why: Hour begins with a vowel sound.

zh: 可數與不可數 much / many
title: Much, Many & A Lot Of
sub: Counting things you can count — and measuring things you can't.

form.p: many + countable   ·   much + uncountable   ·   a lot of + both

uses.d: If you can count them one by one, use many.

ex.s: How many students are in your class?

uses.d: Water, time, money, rice — no counting, so use much.
Countable or uncountable, positive or negative — always safe.

ex.s: There is a lot of homework today.

mistakes.no: How much books do you have?
mistakes.yes: How many books do you have?
mistakes.why: Books are countable → many.

mistakes.yes: There are a lot of people here.
mistakes.why: People is countable; much doesn't fit.

mistakes.yes: I have a lot of homework.
mistakes.why: Homework is uncountable — no s, no many.

tip: Can you count it one by one? Yes → many. No → much. Positive sentence or not sure? A lot of is always safe.

q.q: There aren't ___ chairs in the room.

q.sent: She drinks much water every day .
q.why: In positive sentences, a lot of sounds natural.

q.sent: How many brothers do you have

q.why: A lot of works with countables like friends.

q.q: How ___ people are coming to the party?

q.sent: I don't have many money with me .

title: There Is / There Are
sub: Saying that something exists — the natural way to describe places.

form.p: There is + singular   ·   There are + plural
ex: There are two banks on this street.

uses.d: Use there is / there are to mention something for the first time.

ex.s: There is a park near my house.
There are thirty students in the class.
There is some milk in the fridge.

uses.d: Make negatives with isn't / aren't, usually followed by any.

ex.s: There aren't any seats on this train.

uses.d: Move is / are before there to ask questions.

ex.s: Is there a pharmacy near here? — Yes, there is.

mistakes.why: Plural noun → there are.

mistakes.no: There are a lot of traffic.
mistakes.yes: There is a lot of traffic.
mistakes.why: Traffic is uncountable → there is.

mistakes.no: Have a park near my home.
mistakes.yes: There is a park near my home.
mistakes.why: English uses there is, not have, for existence.

tip: Look at the noun after the verb — it decides everything. A / one thing → is; two or more → are; stuff you can't count → is.

q.q: ___ a good bakery on this street.
q.why: A bakery is singular → there is.
Eggs is plural, question form → are there.

q.q: There ___ a lot of people at the night market.
There ___ some water in the bottle.

q.sent: There are two cats under the bed
There is five chairs in the room .
q.why: Five chairs is plural → there are.

q.sent: Is there any restaurants open now ?

title: Count & Non-count Nouns
sub: Things you can count one by one — and things you can only measure.

form.p: count: a cat, two cats · non-count: water, rice (no plural)

uses.d: You can count them: use a / an and make them plural.
Liquids, materials and ideas you can't count. No a / an, no plural -s.

uses.t: Count them with a unit or container
uses.d: To count a non-count noun, add a unit word: a glass of, a piece of…

mistakes.why: Information is non-count — no -s.

mistakes.yes: She gave me some advice / a piece of advice.
mistakes.why: Advice is non-count — no a / an.
Apples are countable → How many.

tip: Can you say 'two ___s'? Then it's countable (How many?). If not — water, rice, money, advice — it's non-count (How much?).

q.why: Water can't be counted one by one → non-count.

q.q: How ___ students are in the class?
Please buy a ___ of milk. (container word)
q.why: Milk is non-count; count it with a carton / bottle / glass of…

q.sent: She has many homeworks tonight .

q.why: Bread is non-count; count it as loaves of bread.

q.sent: Can I have an advice ?
q.why: Advice is non-count — no a / an.

title: Possessives: my, mine & John's
sub: Three ways to show that something belongs to someone.

form.p: my / your… + noun · mine / yours… (alone) · noun + 's

uses.d: my, your, his, her, its, our, their come before a noun.
mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs replace 'my + noun'. No noun after them.
Add 's to a name or person. For a plural noun already ending in -s, add just an apostrophe.

mistakes.why: Before a noun, use my (not me).
its = belonging to it; it's = it is.
Standing alone, use yours (not your).

tip: Before a noun → my / your / his… No noun after → mine / yours / his… A person owns it → add 's. Careful: its (no apostrophe) belongs to it.

q.q: This is ___ bag. (it belongs to Tom)
That book isn't mine. It's ___ . (it belongs to her)

q.sent: These are the children's books
That car is our .
Its a beautiful day today .

title: Reflexive Pronouns
sub: myself, yourself, herself — when the subject and object are the same person.

form.p: …-self / -selves (the action returns to the subject)

uses.t: The subject does the action to itself
uses.d: Use a reflexive pronoun when the doer and the receiver are the same.
singular: myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself · plural: ourselves, yourselves, themselves.
'by myself' means alone or without help.

mistakes.no: I enjoyed me at the party.
mistakes.yes: I enjoyed myself at the party.
mistakes.why: The action returns to I → myself.
The correct form is himself (never 'hisself').
The correct form is themselves.

tip: When the subject and object are the same, use …self / …selves. Singular -self, plural -selves. 'by myself' = alone.

q.q: She looked at ___ in the mirror.
q.why: she → herself (the action returns to her).

q.q: Be careful — don't cut ___ ! (you, one person)

q.sent: I made this cake myself
q.why: I → myself (I did it, no help).

q.sent: The children dressed theirselves .
He can take care of hisself .

title: Indefinite Pronouns
sub: someone, anything, everybody, nowhere — for people, things and places in general.

form.p: some- / any- / every- / no- + -one / -body / -thing / -where

uses.t: some- in positives; any- in negatives & questions
uses.d: Use someone/something in positive sentences; anyone/anything in negatives and questions.
everyone/everything = all of them; no one/nothing = not any.
Everybody, someone, nothing… are singular — use is / was / has.

mistakes.why: With a negative verb (didn't), use anybody — no double negative.
Everybody is singular → is.

mistakes.yes: There isn't anything here. / There is nothing here.
mistakes.why: Don't use two negatives: either 'isn't anything' or 'is nothing'.

tip: some- (positive), any- (negative/question), every- (all), no- (none). They're singular → use is/has. Avoid double negatives (not… anybody).

q.q: There's ___ at the door. Can you check?
I looked, but I couldn't find ___ .
Did you go ___ nice at the weekend? (any- + place)

q.sent: I don't know nobody in this town .
q.why: With don't, use anybody (no double negative).

q.sent: Everyone have a ticket .

zh: 量詞 a cup of / a piece of
title: Partitives
sub: a cup of, a piece of, a loaf of — how to count uncountable things.

form.p: a / an + unit + of + non-count noun

uses.d: Count liquids and food with a container: cup, glass, bottle, bowl.
Count food by its shape or a portion: piece, slice, loaf, bar.
Make the UNIT word plural (not the non-count noun).

mistakes.yes: I'd like a cup of tea, please.
mistakes.why: Tea is non-count — count it with 'a cup of'.

mistakes.yes: two loaves of bread / two pieces of bread
mistakes.why: Bread is non-count; count it with a unit word.
Make the unit plural (pieces), not the non-count noun.

tip: To count a non-count noun, add a unit: a + cup/piece/slice/bottle + of + noun. Make the UNIT plural (two cups of…), not the noun.

q.q: Can I have a ___ of water?

q.why: two slices of pizza (unit is plural).

q.q: Would you like a ___ of cake? (a portion)
She gave me a good piece ___ advice.

q.sent: I drank three cup of tea .
q.why: Make the unit plural: three cups of tea.

q.sent: He bought two bottle of milk .
q.why: Make the unit plural: two bottles of milk.

title: Wh- Questions
sub: Who, what, when, where, why, how — asking for real information.

form.p: Wh-word + do / does / did (or be) + subject + verb

uses.d: Each wh-word hunts for a different kind of answer.
For most verbs, a helper comes after the wh-word.

ex.n: did → verb goes back to base form

uses.t: How, alone or with a friend
uses.d: How pairs with adjectives for size, age, price and more.

mistakes.why: Wh-questions need do / does / did (or be).
After does, the verb goes back to base form.
Be moves before the subject.

tip: Question order is fixed: Wh-word → helper (do / does / did / be) → subject → verb.

q.why: The answer is a time → when.
The answer is a person → who.

q.q: ___ does this bag cost? — Five hundred dollars.

q.sent: Where does she lives now ?
When does the train leave
What time does he goes to bed ?
q.why: Does already carries the -s — the verb stays base.

title: Imperatives
sub: Sit down. Don't worry. Let's go! — commands, instructions and invitations.

form.p: Base verb …   ·   Don't + base verb   ·   Let's + base verb

uses.d: Start with the verb — no subject needed. You is understood.
Don't + base verb tells someone what NOT to do.

uses.t: Let's for suggestions, please for politeness
uses.d: Let's includes yourself; please softens any command.

mistakes.why: Imperatives drop the subject you.
After don't, use the base verb — no to.
Let's + base form.

tip: Start with the verb. Negative? Just put Don't in front. Including yourself? Start with Let's.

q.why: Negative with an adjective → don't be.

q.q: Please ___ (turn) off your phone during the movie.

q.sent: Let's watching a movie tonight .
Don't eat in the library
Turns off the light when you leave .

zh: 連接詞 and / but / so / because
title: And, But, So & Because
sub: Four little words that join ideas — adding, contrasting, resulting and explaining.

form.p: idea 1 + and / but / so / because + idea 2
ex: He stayed home because he was sick.

uses.d: And joins similar ideas; but signals a surprise or opposite.
Cause first, then so, then what happened because of it.

ex.s: It was raining, so we took a taxi.
I forgot my wallet, so I couldn't pay.
The test is tomorrow, so let's review tonight.

uses.d: Because answers why — it introduces the cause.

ex.s: We stayed inside because it was too hot.
Because he practiced daily, he improved fast.

mistakes.no: I was hungry so because I ate.
mistakes.yes: I was hungry, so I ate.
mistakes.why: Pick one connector, not two.

mistakes.yes: I went to bed early because I was tired.
mistakes.why: Because needs a main sentence — it can't stand alone.

mistakes.no: He was sick, but he went to the doctor.
mistakes.yes: He was sick, so he went to the doctor.
mistakes.why: Seeing the doctor is the result of being sick → so.

tip: and = plus · but = opposite · so = result · because = reason.

q.q: I wanted to call you, ___ my phone died.
q.why: An obstacle — the opposite of the plan → but.

q.q: She was thirsty, ___ she drank some water.
We wear coats ___ it is cold.
q.why: The cold is the reason → because.

q.sent: I studied hard , because I passed the test .
I like tea but I don't like coffee
q.why: Contrast between the two likes → but.

opts: Because was raining, we stayed home.
We stayed home because it was raining.
We stayed home so because it was raining.
We stayed home because so it was raining.
q.why: Because + full clause, one connector only.

q.sent: The soup was hot , and I waited for it to cool .
q.why: Waiting is the result of the heat → so.

title: Prepositions: In, On, At
sub: The three little words for time and place — and how to pick the right one.

form.p: at + point   ·   on + surface / day   ·   in + space / period

uses.d: At for clock times, on for days and dates, in for longer periods.
At a point, on a surface, in an enclosed space.
Some combinations are fixed — learn them as chunks.

mistakes.why: Days take on.

mistakes.no: He gets up at the morning.
mistakes.yes: He gets up in the morning.
mistakes.why: Parts of the day take in — except at night.
Set phrase: at home.

tip: Zoom out: at a point (7:00, the door) → on a surface or day (Monday, the table) → in a big space or period (July, Taipei, the box).

q.q: The cat is sleeping ___ the sofa.

q.sent: We have English class in Tuesday .
The bank opens at nine in the morning
q.why: At + clock time, in + the morning.

q.sent: She studies at the library on the evening .
q.why: Parts of the day take in.

title: Yes / No Questions
sub: Questions answered with 'Yes' or 'No' — and how to build them.

form.p: Be / Do / Does / Can… + subject + …?

uses.t: With be — move be to the front
uses.d: Put am / is / are before the subject.

uses.t: With other verbs — use do / does
uses.d: Present simple: use do (I / you / we / they) or does (he / she / it) + the base verb.
Answer with the same helping verb — don't repeat the whole sentence.

ex.s: Do you like it? — Yes, I do. / No, I don't.

mistakes.why: With be, don't add do — just move be to the front.
After does, use the base verb (like).
Start present-simple questions with Do / Does.

tip: Be verb? → move it to the front. Any other verb? → start with Do / Does / Did + the base verb.

q.why: like is an ordinary verb → Do you like…?
he + ordinary verb → Does he speak…?

q.q: ___ they at the party last night? (be)

q.sent: Do you have a pen
Does your brother plays soccer ?

q.q: Best short answer to 'Can you swim?'
q.why: Answer with the same helping verb: Yes, I can.

q.sent: Are you have a car ?
q.why: have is an ordinary verb → Do you have a car?

title: Wh- Questions (Past)
sub: Asking who, what, where, when and why about the past — with did.

form.p: Wh- + did + subject + base verb …?

uses.d: For most past questions, use did + the base verb (not the past form).
If the verb is was / were, don't use did. Put was / were after the Wh- word.

uses.t: Who as the subject — no did
uses.d: When Who or What asks about the doer (the subject), use the past verb directly.

mistakes.why: Order: Wh- + did + subject + base verb.
After did, use the base verb (go), not went.
With were, put it before the subject; no did.

tip: Most past questions: Wh- + DID + subject + base verb. But with was / were, skip did. And when Who is the doer, use the past verb directly.

q.why: past question → What did you do…?
be verb → Where were you born? (you → were)

q.q: Who ___ the cake? (eat, past — Who = subject)
q.hint: no did; use the past verb
q.why: Who is the subject → ate (no did).

q.sent: When did the train leave
Why did the baby cried ?

q.why: How was the weather? (asking about its condition)

q.sent: What time did you woke up ?

title: Tag Questions
sub: The little checking question at the end: '…, isn't it?'

form.p: positive sentence + negative tag? · negative sentence + positive tag?

uses.d: If the sentence is positive, the tag is negative. Use the same helping verb.
If the sentence is negative, the tag is positive.
Use be, or the helper (do / does / did, can, will…), and match the pronoun to the subject.

mistakes.why: Match the verb: are → aren't; you → you.
The subject is she, so the tag pronoun is she.
Positive sentence → negative tag.

tip: Positive sentence → negative tag, and the reverse. Use the same helping verb, and match the pronoun (Mary → she).

q.sent: He is tired isn't he
You are coming , don't you ?
Maria isn't here , isn't she ?
q.why: Negative sentence → positive tag: is she.

zh: 時間介系詞 at / in / on
title: Time: At, In, On
sub: Choosing at, in or on for clock times, days and months.

form.p: at + time · on + day/date · in + month/year/part of day

uses.d: Use at for exact times and a few fixed phrases.
Use on for days of the week and specific dates.
Use in for months, seasons, years and parts of the day.

mistakes.why: Days of the week take on.
Months take in.

mistakes.no: I get up at the morning.
mistakes.yes: I get up in the morning.
mistakes.why: Parts of the day take in (but note: at night).

tip: at = a point (a clock time). on = a day or date. in = a longer box of time (month, year, season). Watch out: at night.

q.q: The cat sleeps a lot ___ night.

q.sent: School finishes in 3:30 .
Her wedding is at Saturday .

title: Place & Movement
sub: Prepositions for where things are (in, on, under) and where they go (to, into, across).

form.p: place: in / on / under / between · movement: to / into / out of / across

uses.d: in (inside), on (a surface), under, next to, between, behind, in front of.

ex.s: The lamp is between the two beds.

uses.d: to (a destination), into / out of, up / down, across, through, along.
Use in/on for position; into/onto for movement to that position.

mistakes.why: For movement inside, use into.
arrive IN a city (not 'arrive to').

mistakes.no: The bird flew threw the window.
mistakes.yes: The bird flew through the window.
mistakes.why: through (movement), not 'threw' (past of throw).

tip: Position → in / on / under / between. Movement → to / into / out of / across / through. Note: arrive in a place, not 'arrive to'.

q.why: position (where it is) → under the table.

q.q: We walked ___ the bridge to the other side.
q.why: movement to the other side → across.

q.q: The cat is hiding ___ the bed. (position, underneath)

q.sent: He put the book on the shelf
They went in the cave to explore .

q.why: arrive IN a city → arrived in Tokyo.

q.sent: The dog jumped in the sofa .
q.why: movement onto a surface → onto the sofa.

title: Questions: Present Continuous
sub: Asking what is happening right now — Are you…? What are you doing?

form.p: (Wh-) + am / is / are + subject + V-ing?

uses.t: Yes/No questions — move be to the front
uses.d: Put am / is / are before the subject; keep the -ing verb.

uses.t: Wh- questions — Wh + be + subject + V-ing
uses.d: Start with the question word, then be, then the subject and -ing verb.
Answer with be — don't repeat the -ing verb.

ex.s: Are you studying? — Yes, I am. / No, I'm not.

mistakes.why: Present continuous questions use be (are), not do.
Order: Wh- + be + subject + V-ing.
Keep the -ing form: playing.

tip: Present continuous question = (Wh-) + am/is/are + subject + verb-ing. Use be, not do. Keep the -ing.

q.sent: Why is the dog barking
Do you listening to me ?

q.q: Best short answer to 'Is it raining?'
q.why: Answer with be: Yes, it is.

q.sent: What is he do right now ?

title: Can & Could
sub: Ability, permission and polite requests — can, can't, could and couldn't.

form.p: subject + can / could + base verb

uses.d: Use can for present ability, could for past ability. Always + the base verb.

ex.s: He could read at the age of four.

uses.d: Ask permission with Can I / Could I. Could is a little more polite.
Ask someone to do something with Can you / Could you. Could you is politer.

mistakes.why: After can, use the base verb — no 'to'.
can never adds -s; it's the same for everyone.
After could, use the base verb (speak).

tip: can / could + base verb (no 'to', no -s). can = now, could = past ability or a politer version. Could you…? is the polite request.

q.q: When I was young, I ___ run very fast.
Which is the most polite request?
opts: Can you give me a pen?
Could you give me a pen, please?
q.why: Could you… please? is the politest.

q.q: She ___ swim, so she stays near the shore. (negative ability)

q.sent: Can I borrow your book
q.why: Can + I + base verb for permission.

q.sent: He can to drive a car .
q.why: After can, use the base verb — no 'to'.

q.sent: My sister cans speak English well .

title: Should & Ought To
sub: Giving advice — what is a good idea to do.

form.p: subject + should / ought to + base verb

uses.d: Use should + base verb to say what is a good idea. shouldn't for a bad idea.
ought to means the same as should. Note the 'to' before the verb.
Ask 'Should I…?' to get advice.

mistakes.why: should + base verb — no 'to'.
ought needs 'to': ought to sleep.
should never takes -s.

tip: should + base verb (no 'to'). ought TO + base verb (with 'to'). Both give advice. Question: Should I…?

q.q: You look tired. You ___ go to bed.
It's raining. We ___ take an umbrella.
You ___ smoke — it's bad for you. (negative advice)

q.sent: Should I call the doctor
You should to eat breakfast .

q.why: What should I do? asks for advice.

q.sent: He ought study harder .

title: Must & Have To
sub: Rules and necessity — and what you don't need to do.

form.p: subject + must / have to + base verb

uses.t: must — a strong rule or a personal need
uses.d: Use must + base verb for strong rules and things you feel are necessary.

ex.s: You must stop at a red light.

uses.d: have to means the same as must. Use has to for he / she / it; had to in the past.

uses.t: don't have to = it is NOT necessary
uses.d: 'don't have to' means there is no need — different from mustn't (not allowed).

ex.s: You don't have to come — it's optional.

mistakes.why: must + base verb — no 'to'.
he / she / it → has to.
For 'no need', use don't have to (not don't must).

tip: must + base verb (no 'to'). have to / has to = necessity. Careful: mustn't = NOT allowed, but don't have to = NO need — very different!

q.q: Students ___ wear a uniform. It's a school rule.
My mother is a nurse, so she ___ work at night sometimes.
Tomorrow is a holiday, so we ___ go to school.
Yesterday I ___ to wait a long time. (past of have to)

q.sent: You must not touch the paintings
He must to leave early .
She have to finish her homework .

title: May & Might
sub: Saying something is possible — and asking politely for permission.

form.p: subject + may / might + base verb

uses.d: Use may or might + base verb to say something is possible (you're not sure).

ex.s: I might not go to the party.

uses.d: May I…? is a polite (slightly formal) way to ask permission.
Just may / might + the base verb.

mistakes.why: might + base verb — no 'to'.
may never takes -s.
After might, use the base verb (come).

tip: may / might + base verb = perhaps / possibly. May I…? is polite permission. No -s, no 'to'.

q.q: Take a coat — it ___ get cold later.
I'm not sure. I ___ not go. (possibility)

q.sent: They might be at home
It may to snow tomorrow .

q.q: 'It ___ be true, but I'm not sure.'

q.sent: He mays win the prize .

title: Would Like
sub: A polite way to say what you want — and to offer and invite.

form.p: subject + would like + noun / to + base verb

uses.d: Use would like ('d like) instead of want to be polite. + a noun, or + to + verb.

ex.s: I'd like a glass of water.
I'd like to book a table.
She'd like to learn the guitar.

uses.d: Offer with Would you like + noun; invite with Would you like to + verb.
Answer offers with 'Yes, please.' or 'No, thank you.'

ex.s: Would you like more? — No, thank you.

mistakes.why: 'I would like…' is a statement — no question mark.

mistakes.yes: I would like to go home.
mistakes.why: Before a verb, use 'to': would like to go.

mistakes.no: Do you would like some tea?
mistakes.why: Start the question with Would (no 'do').

tip: would like = a polite 'want'. + a noun, or + TO + verb. Offer with 'Would you like…?' Answer: 'Yes, please.' / 'No, thank you.'

q.q: I'd like ___ a table for two, please.
Polite answer to 'Would you like more cake?'
q.why: Offers are answered with 'No, thank you.'

q.q: She ___ like to visit Japan one day. (short form of would after 'She')

q.sent: I would like to order now
Would you like drink something ?
q.why: Before a verb, use 'to': like to drink.

q.sent: Do you would like some help ?

title: Should Have
sub: Looking back — the right thing to do, but it didn't happen.

form.p: subject + should have + past participle (V3)

uses.t: should have + V3 — a past regret
uses.d: Use should have + the past participle to say the right thing to do in the past — but you didn't.

ex.n: a good idea, but you didn't

uses.d: Use shouldn't have + V3 for something you did that was a bad idea.
In speaking, should have is often said 'should've'. Never write 'should of'!

mistakes.why: It's should HAVE, never 'should of' — they just sound alike.
Use the past participle: gone (not went).
After should have, use the past participle (studied).

tip: should have + V3 (past participle) = the right thing in the past, but it didn't happen. In speech: 'should've' — never 'should of'.

q.q: I failed the test. I ___ harder.
I'm so full. I ___ have eaten so much. (negative)
q.why: shouldn't have eaten = it was a mistake.

q.sent: You should have told me
He should have went home .
q.why: the past participle of go is gone.

q.q: 'I should have brought an umbrella' means…
opts: I didn't bring one, and I regret it.
q.why: should have = didn't do it, now regret.

q.sent: You should of studied more .

title: Participle Adjectives: -ed vs -ing
sub: bored or boring? The -ed feeling vs the -ing cause.

form.p: -ed = how someone feels · -ing = what causes the feeling

uses.d: Use the -ed adjective to describe how someone feels.
Use the -ing adjective for the thing that causes the feeling.
A person is -ed BY something -ing.

mistakes.why: To say how YOU feel, use -ed: bored. (I am boring = I make others bored!)
The movie causes the feeling → -ing: boring.
How she feels → -ed: interested.

tip: -ed = the feeling (I'm bored). -ing = the cause (it's boring). If a person feels it, use -ed; if a thing causes it, use -ing.

q.why: the trip causes the feeling → tiring (-ing).

q.q: After the long trip, I was very ___ .
This book is really ___ . I can't stop reading! (-ing)
The children were ___ by the magic show. (-ed, feeling)

q.sent: I was very boring during the meeting .
The news was so shocked .
q.why: The news causes the feeling → shocking (-ing).

title: Collocations: Have, Take, Get
sub: Words that naturally go together — have a shower, take a break, get better.

form.p: learn these as whole phrases

uses.d: 'have' goes with meals, some activities and experiences.

ex.s: have a shower / a rest / a good time

uses.d: 'take' goes with these common actions.

ex.s: take a photo / a break / a taxi

uses.d: 'get' often means become, receive, or arrive.

mistakes.why: Meals go with 'have': have breakfast.
The natural pair is take a photo.
The natural pair is have a shower.

tip: Learn these as fixed pairs: have (meals, a shower, a rest), take (a photo, a break, a taxi, medicine), get (ready, better, home).

q.why: the natural pair is take a break.

q.q: Can you ___ a photo of us? (the natural verb)
I need to ___ a shower before we go. (the natural verb)

q.sent: Please make a taxi to the airport .
q.why: the natural pair is take a taxi.

q.sent: I take breakfast at eight every day .

zh: 運動與活動 do / go / play
title: Do, Go & Play (Activities)
sub: Which verb for which activity — play tennis, go swimming, do yoga.

form.p: play + ball games · go + -ing activities · do + other exercise

uses.d: Use 'play' for sports with a ball or a game/opponent.
Use 'go' + the -ing form for many activities (often outdoors).
Use 'do' for exercise without a ball, and some tasks.

mistakes.why: Activities ending in -ing take 'go': go swimming.
Ball games take 'play': play tennis.
Exercise without a ball takes 'do': do yoga.

tip: play + ball games & instruments (play tennis, play the piano). go + -ing activities (go swimming). do + exercise/tasks (do yoga, do homework).

q.q: Let's ___ shopping this weekend. (the right verb)
He can ___ the piano beautifully. (the right verb)

q.sent: They play running in the park .
I go karate twice a week .
q.why: exercise without a ball → do karate.
